content_voiceover: This algorithm outlines when and how to treat large granular lymphocyte leukemia. Since the disease is often indolent, treatment is reserved for specific indications: absolute neutrophil count below 0.5, hemoglobin below 10 or need for red cell transfusion, platelets below 50, autoimmune disease with T-LGLL requiring therapy, symptomatic splenomegaly, severe B symptoms, pulmonary artery hypertension secondary to LGLL, or an ANC below 1500 with documented T-LGLL and recurrent infections. If none of these are present, the recommendation is simply to observe. When treatment is indicated, first line therapy centers on oral cyclophosphamide or methotrexate, ideally within a clinical trial, and in select circumstances managing the underlying cytopenia alone may be reasonable without targeting the clone directly. Response is assessed at four months. Complete or partial responders continue treatment or move to intermittent therapy. Non-responders switch to an alternate first line agent or to ruxolitinib. Patients who are refractory to all first line options move to second line therapy, with clinical trial, cyclosporine, ruxolitinib if not previously used, or purine analogues preferred, and alemtuzumab, given subcutaneously or intravenously, as another recommended option.
keypoints: Treatment reserved for cytopenias, symptomatic splenomegaly, severe B symptoms, or LGLL-associated autoimmune disease/PAH
First-line: oral cyclophosphamide or methotrexate; response assessed at 4 months
Non-response or relapse: alternate first-line agent or ruxolitinib
Refractory to all first-line therapy: clinical trial, cyclosporine, ruxolitinib, purine analogues, or alemtuzumab
keypoint_voiceover: The board takeaway is that LGLL is only treated when there are specific cytopenic, symptomatic, or autoimmune indications, otherwise you observe. First line therapy is oral cyclophosphamide or methotrexate, response is checked at four months, and refractory disease escalates to agents like ruxolitinib, cyclosporine, purine analogues, or alemtuzumab.
